quote: So when an expert says they’re 99% confident, it only happens about 70% of the time.
content: Forecasters with fast feedback are the exception. For the experts who opine without it, the number is close to right. In Tetlock's twenty-year study of political and economic experts, outcomes the experts called impossible happened about 15% of the time, and outcomes they called sure things failed to happen more than a quarter of the time (Tetlock 2005, Expert Political Judgment, book, no DOI). Clinicians did no better. Physicians' probabilities of pneumonia were badly miscalibrated when checked against X-rays (Christensen-Szalanski & Bushyhead 1981). "Expert" was too broad, since Murphy & Winkler's forecasters are real. But the experts the mother would meet on television are Tetlock's, and for them "99% means about 70%" is roughly what was measured.

quote: Attitude polarization. Exposing subjects to an apparently balanced set of pro and con arguments will exaggerate their initial polarization.
content: The polarization item failed, as Guess & Coppock showed, and it should carry that flag. But the title does not rest on it. It rests on the sixth prediction, the sophistication effect, and on the processing biases, which the essay's own gloss puts first: "They have more ammunition with which to argue against anything they don't like." Those replicated. A follow-up by Taber's group reproduced the prior-attitude and disconfirmation effects (Taber, Cann & Kucsova 2009), and a meta-analysis of partisan bias in evaluating identical information found it robust and roughly equal on both sides (Ditto et al. 2019). Knowledge turned into ammunition does not require that balanced evidence makes people more extreme. It requires that they evaluate the evidence asymmetrically, and they do.

quote: one of the primary ways that people with high mental agility end up stupid, in Stanovich’s “dysrationalia” sense of stupidity
content: The 2008 paper Fable cites is titled "On the relative independence of thinking biases and cognitive ability." Its finding is that a range of classic effects, anchoring and framing among them, showed no association with cognitive ability when tested between subjects, the way they appear in life (Stanovich & West 2008). The negative correlations Fable reports come from within-subject designs, where the right answer is visible. "Dysrationalia" is Stanovich's own coinage for intelligent people failing to think rationally, which is the essay's usage. With myside bias also unrelated to ability, as Fable grants, the essay's claim follows: mental agility supplies the ammunition and nothing prevents it being fired.

quote: Whether I do it on paper, or in speech, I now try to never mention calibration and overconfidence unless I have first talked about disconfirmation bias, motivated skepticism, sophisticated arguers, and dysrationalia in the mentally agile.
content: What the essay does is not bare forewarning. It trains the recognition of motivated skepticism in oneself before handing over a weapon usable on others. That kind of intervention has a record. In controlled trials, a single training session, a video or an interactive game, reduced confirmation bias, the bias blind spot and other biases, and the effects persisted two to three months later (Morewedge et al. 2015). Lilienfeld and colleagues' review says the same: bare awareness fails, and training aimed at one's own reasoning does better (Lilienfeld, Ammirati & Landfield 2009). The essay did not measure its lecture order, and it should have. The order it chose is the one the evidence favours.
